# ECON 0100 | Exercise C2 | Taxes & Subsidies

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

In recent years Hogsmeade has seen a proliferation of candy shops selling smoked toffees. The Demand (marginal benefit) curve and Supply (marginal cost) curve for smoked toffee can be represented by the following relationships.

$$
D: P_B = 20 - \frac{1}{2} Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 2 + Q_S
$$

Due to the metabolic issues among the younger generation of wizards in the community resulting from the consumption of these high glycemic index treats, the Ministry of Magic imposed a 3 Coin tax on the sale of smoked toffee.

::: solution

**a)** With no tax: Yes. With the tax: Yes. Total Surplus to buyer and seller: $1$ Coin. Tax paid: $3$ Coins. Total Surplus (with the Ministry): $4$ Coins. Deadweight Loss: $0$.

**b)** With no tax: Yes. With the tax: No. Total Surplus to buyer and seller: $0$. Tax paid: $0$. Total Surplus (with the Ministry): $0$. Deadweight Loss: $2$ Coins.

**a)** The buyer values the toffee at $16$ and it costs the seller $12$, so without the tax there is $4$ of surplus to share and the trade happens. With the tax, $3$ of that $4$ goes to the Ministry, leaving $1$ for the buyer and seller: still positive, so they still trade. Counting the Ministry’s $3$ as surplus (it is spent on something), total surplus is $1 + 3 = 4$, the same $4$ as before. The tax moved surplus around but did not destroy any, so this exchange carries no deadweight loss.

**b)** Without the tax, $14 > 12$ and the trade happens, creating $2$ of surplus. With the tax, the buyer’s price would have to cover the seller’s $12$ plus $3$ for the Ministry, $15$, more than the $14$ the buyer is willing to pay. So no trade: no surplus to the buyer and seller, and no tax paid either, since nothing is sold. The $2$ this trade would have created is simply gone. That is the deadweight loss of a tax: it comes from the trades it prevents, not from the trades it taxes.

:::

Who bears more of the tax? *buyers · sellers · equal*

::::: solution

Pre-Tax Price $\hat{P}$: $14$ Coins. Pre-Tax Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $12$ toffees. Buyer’s Price $P_b$: $15$. Seller’s Price $P_s$: $12$. Post-Tax Quantity $Q^{Tax}$: $10$. Dead Weight Loss: $3$ Coins. Tax Incidence on Buyers: $1$. Tax Incidence on Sellers: $2$. Who bears more: sellers.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Before the tax, buyers and sellers face one price:

$$
20 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 2 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 12, \quad P = 14
$$

With the tax, the buyer price sits $3$ above the seller price. Slide the $3$-Coin wedge in from the left until it gets stuck between the curves:

$$
P_b = 3 + P_s \quad\Rightarrow\quad 20 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 3 + (2 + Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 10
$$

so $P_b = 20 - 5 = 15$ and $P_s = 2 + 10 = 12$.

:::

::: column

![Tax equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Incidence: buyers pay $15 - 14 = 1$ more than before and sellers receive $14 - 12 = 2$ less, so sellers bear more of the tax. Supply is steeper (less elastic) than demand here, and the side that can adjust less bears more.

Welfare areas: consumer surplus shrinks to the triangle above $15$, producer surplus to the triangle below $12$, and the rectangle between the two prices over the $10$ toffees still sold is the Ministry’s revenue, $3 \times 10 = 30$. The triangle between the curves over the $2$ toffees no longer sold is the deadweight loss:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (12 - 10) = 3
$$

:::::

## Q3 | Subsidy Equilibrium

Now suppose that instead of the tax, the Ministry of Magic pays a 3 Coin subsidy on every smoked toffee sold. Use a graph and algebra to discuss the impact of the subsidy on the market.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Buyer’s Price ($P_b$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

Seller’s Price ($P_s$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::::

:::: {.columns .continued gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Post-Sub Quantity ($Q^{Sub}$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

Deadweight Loss (*DWL*):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::::

::::: solution

Buyer’s Price $P_b$: $13$ Coins. Seller’s Price $P_s$: $16$ Coins. Post-Sub Quantity $Q^{Sub}$: $14$ toffees. Deadweight Loss: $3$ Coins.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

A subsidy is the tax wedge turned around: the seller now receives $3$ more than the buyer pays, so the wedge sits to the *right* of the no-policy equilibrium:

$$
P_s = 3 + P_b \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2 + Q = 3 + (20 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 14
$$

so $P_b = 20 - 7 = 13$ and $P_s = 2 + 14 = 16$.

:::

::: column

![Subsidy equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Both sides are better off: buyers pay $1$ less and sellers receive $2$ more. But the Ministry pays $3 \times 14 = 42$, more than the two gains together, because the $13$th and $14$th toffees cost more to make ($15$ and $16$) than buyers value them ($13.5$ and $13$). They trade only because the Ministry pays the difference. The triangle between the curves over those $2$ toffees is the deadweight loss:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (14 - 12) = 3
$$

:::::
